subject.title: Human Condition
subject.author: Thom Gunn
subject.text:
Now it is fog, I walk
Contained within my coat;
No castle more cut off
By reason of its moat:
Only the sentry's cough,
The mercenaries' talk.

The street lamps, visible,
Drop no light on the ground,
But press beams painfully
In a yard of fog around.
I am condemned to be
An individual.

In the established border
There balances a mere
Pinpoint of consciousness.
I stay, or start from, here:
No fog makes more or less
The neighbouring disorder.

Particular, I must
Find out the limitation
Of mind and universe,
To pick thought and sensation
And turn to my own use
Disordered hate or lust.

I seek, to break, my span.
I am my one touchstone.
This is a test more hard
Than any ever known.
And thus I keep my guard
On that which makes me man.

Much is unknowable.
No problem shall be faced
Until the problem is;
I, born to fog, to waste,
Walk through hypothesis,
An individual.

title: One Word Short of Free
standfirst: Sartre's most famous sentence says a man is condemned to be free. Thom Gunn's 1955 poem borrows half of it and drops the rest, written in the first unsettled year of an American life that had rather more riding on it than a philosophy seminar.

sections.heading: The Sentence With the End Cut Off
sections.body:
Jean-Paul Sartre's best-known sentence turns on a single word. In the 1946 lecture that reached English readers two years later in [Philip Mairet's translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialism_Is_a_Humanism), Sartre told his audience that man is [condemned to be free](https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/sartre/works/exist/sartre.htm) — condemned, because he did not make himself, and free, because once thrown into the world he answers for everything he does. The condemnation and the liberty arrive in the same breath; take away either half and the sentence says something else entirely.

Gunn's poem takes half of it and stops there: *I am condemned to be / An individual.* No mention of freedom. Sartre's condemned man gets liberty as the compensation for having no creator; Gunn's gets nothing but the fact of being separate, cut off, as the poem's own first image has it, like a castle behind its own moat. It is the bleakest reading of Sartre available in 1955 — arrived at by removing the one word that redeems the philosophy.

sections.heading: The Reason He Didn't Give
sections.body:
"Human Condition" appeared in [Poetry's June 1955 issue](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poetrymagazine/poems/26688/human-condition), edited from Chicago by Karl Shapiro — within Gunn's first year in the United States. He had crossed the Atlantic in September 1954 on a graduate fellowship to study under Yvor Winters at Stanford. That was the reason on paper. The real one, by Gunn's own later account, was that he [wished to stay near](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v40/n17/colm-toibin/on-not-being-sylvia-plath) Mike Kitay, the Cambridge classmate he had met at a cast party in December 1952, and applied for American scholarships to do it.

That reason was not one he could put in a fellowship application, still less a poem, in 1954: homosexuality was a criminal offence in Britain and in most of the United States. When Kitay went on to do his military service, the army [investigated their relationship](https://lareviewofbooks.org/article/a-masque-of-difference-and-likeness-on-michael-notts-thom-gunn/) as part of a wider inquiry into suspected homosexuality in his unit; Gunn wrote to friends of his fear for them both, of deportation for himself and a court-martial for Kitay. Nothing came of it. But that is the kind of year "Human Condition" was written into — a newly arrived foreigner describing himself as a castle cut off by its own moat, guarded by a sentry and mercenaries he never names.

sections.heading: A Word Given No Rhyme
sections.body:
The poem locks itself to one pattern across all six of its six-line stanzas: a rhyme scheme in which the first and last lines answer each other, then the second and fourth, then the third and fifth — an envelope that closes twice inside itself before starting over. Onto that pattern Gunn hangs a small arsenal of siege vocabulary: a castle, a moat, a sentry, mercenaries in the opening stanza, and, five stanzas later, the same idea returning as *I keep my guard*.

The poem's key word gets no such symmetry. *Individual* closes stanza two and stanza six, and both times its rhyme partner is approximate rather than true — *visible*, *unknowable* — where every other line-one-and-six pair in the poem rhymes cleanly: *walk/talk*, *border/disorder*, *must/lust*, *span/man*. The one word the poem is actually about is the one word its own form declines to resolve.

sections.heading: New Lines, Old Fog
sections.body:
A year after "Human Condition" appeared in *Poetry*, Robert Conquest anthologised Gunn in [New Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Movement_%28literature%29) (1956) alongside Philip Larkin, Kingsley Amis, Donald Davie and John Wain — the book that gave English criticism the label "the Movement," and for a while, its reading of Gunn. The Movement's stated taste ran the other way from a fogbound monologue built on a French philosopher's lecture: plain, traditionally formed English verse, wary of [verbal obscurity and metaphysical pretentiousness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Movement_%28literature%29), more at home with a nostalgic, faintly rural English scene than with a castle standing in for a state of mind.

The fit was never quite exact, and it did not last. By the time New Lines reached readers, Gunn was in California, publishing in an American little magazine rather than the London journals that mattered to Conquest's group, studying under a formalist, Yvor Winters, whose own tastes had nothing to do with Movement orthodoxy. A label built for poets writing about English trains and English churchyards had, in this one case, already been overtaken by a different country's fog.

sections.heading: The Pose He Later Admitted To
sections.body:
"Human Condition" and "On the Move" ended up between the same covers, in [The Sense of Movement](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/3751853-the-sense-of-movement) (1957) — the fogbound pedestrian keeping his guard, and, a few poems later, the leather-jacketed motorcyclist revving an engine toward roughly the same existential purpose. Gunn himself eventually named what both were doing. Looking back on his early work, he described building a crude theory of what he called "pose," drawing, in his own words, ["partly on the dramatics of John Donne"](https://kenyonreview.org/kr-online-issue/2008-summer/selections/existentialism-and-homosexuality-in-gunns-early-poetry/), on Yeats's theory of the mask, and most on the behaviour of Stendhal's heroes — the conviction that everyone plays a part whether they know it or not, so one might as well design the part deliberately, with Sartre folded in later as reinforcement rather than source.

Read that way, *condemned to be / An individual* is less a confession than a chosen line, delivered by a poet whom Cambridge and Stendhal had already prepared to speak in poses before he had worked out, in print, exactly what he needed a pose to cover. The fog, the moat, the guard he keeps: not a report on how Gunn felt in his first year in America so much as a part he had decided, deliberately, to play in it.
